doc.title: Larry Gold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2025

chapter: The Philly Sound and its makers
title: Learning on the job and acceptance by Gamble, Huff and Bell
summary: Early uncertainty, Whitehead's Golden Child nickname, Kenny Gamble's regard, and his son working in Gold's studio.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: I read a quote from let's see, who said it — Fred Wesley, when I spoke to him. He said this phrase probably six times in the interview talking about writing for James Brown he said, "I didn't know what I was doing." And he kept saying it, like — and I felt like saying, "Well yes you did." But have you ever been in a situation early on that you didn't feel like you knew what you were doing?

Absolutely. You learn on the job. That's what Fred means. But Fred was a great player. And he knew all about that stuff, he had grown up listening to those records. Come on. You know? But yeah I mean my early on I would look for — I would wait for Tommy Bell to smile or Gamble & Huff to say damn that's nice or McFadden and Whitehead to come in and start dancing in the studio in front of the strings. You know? All of a sudden I said, "I take it you like it." They said, "Yeah we do." I mean Whitehead used to call me the Golden Child.
Well you had no issues being accepted into that if it was a circle, but I'll call it a circle?

You know I got to, as the years went on I got more and more accepted into it. You know Kenny Gamble, I've seen him like recently and he said "Boy I wish I would have known how talented you were when we were kids." Because he thought I was just a cello player in one way. But then as the years went on he saw, and then he used to come to my studio, you know, and in one way, and then when you know his son — his son came and worked for me for a little while. Kenny called me up and said he didn't have a studio and he wasn't really into everyday record business, and he said, "My son's dying to work for someone who makes records all the time." And he came and he worked as an assistant engineer. In those days we used to have — you had to EQ the tape recorders, you had to align the tape recorders, you had to do — you know we tried to teach Caliph how to do all that and he was real happy being here. And Kenny just expressed to me the fact that he wished that he would have known the breadth of my talents back in those days. But © Fillius Jazz Archive 12

you know what? I was a shy person in a way. You know I didn't want to — I did open my mouth too much. I have to say, I wasn't that shy. But I didn't want to overstep my bounds in my relationship with Gamble, Huff and Bell.
